scenario_extra.statement: The IMV uplift costs {{SPINE_COST_A}} and the IRPF cut costs {{SPINE_COST_B}}. They are not the same size: about {{SPINE_GAP_PCT}} per cent apart, with {{SPINE_CHEAPER}} the cheaper of the two. Two reforms of different size cannot be compared on their absolute welfare effects, because the larger one moves more money and so scores higher at ε=0 whatever its targeting. The comparison here is therefore per euro of exchequer cost. On that measure the two are exactly equally efficient at ε=0, where the welfare measure is simply the money moved: 1.000 against 1.000. As ε rises the bottom-targeted transfer pulls ahead, reaching 1.601 against 0.785 at ε=1 and 2.590 against 0.709 at ε=2, because a euro reaching a poorer household counts for more while the tax cut's value falls away. The same pattern holds in all three EU tools. It is a statement about ratios, not about which reform is larger, and the per-euro columns of the table below are where to read it.

ui.single_note: Single-reform explorer. Exactly one control is active at a time: moving any slider resets the others to baseline. Combinations are not supported: the response surface is built from single-reform grids, which cannot represent how two reforms interact, so the tool will not let you set two at once. Spain has no binary toggle.
ui.epsnote: ε = inequality aversion. 0 = every € counts equally; 1 = a € to a household at or below the poverty line counts about 1.7 times as much; 2 = about 2.8 times. Those are the maxima: living standards are floored at 60% of the median before the weight is taken. ε is a value judgement you set; the welfare number updates live as you move it. See the Home tab for detail.
ui.welfare_measure: What this measures: the euro value of the reform's effect on household welfare, where a euro of gain to a poorer household counts for more than the same euro to a richer one (ε sets how much more). It is distributionally weighted euros, not simply the total euros gained. Shown in 2024 euros.
ui.scenarios_epsnote: ε = inequality aversion. 0 = every € counts equally; 1 = a € to a household at or below the poverty line counts about 1.7 times as much; 2 = about 2.8 times. Those are the maxima: living standards are floored at 60% of the median before the weight is taken. The scenario ranking reorders as ε rises. See the Home tab for detail.

unemployment_caveat: The exchequer cost of the unemployment scenarios EXCLUDES the contributory unemployment-benefit response and therefore UNDERSTATES the true fiscal cost: the model's les-flip mechanism removes earnings but does not confer unemployment-benefit eligibility.
capacity_caveat: The capacity and shock model is INDICATIVE: it uses UK-derived operational parameters (demand elasticities and staff ratios), scaled to this country's own {{UNITS}} but not Spain-calibrated. The shock magnitudes are computed points on this country's own surface, but the share of {{UNITS}} losing an earner is the UK's own share, applied to this country's own WORKING-AGE unit count so that the base matches the one the UK measures the share on. Treat the demand, utilisation and gap figures as order-of-magnitude, not a local forecast.
provenance: EU-SILC 2024 wave; income reference year 2023; EUROMOD policy system 2023 (ES_2023). Analyst welfare and distributional results come from the validated response surface; the fiscal figures are the surface's re-emitted net exchequer cost. Analyst monetary values are 2023 nominal EUR shown in 2024 EUR (×1.0289); Provider values are 2024-equivalent EUR. Built on the EU-SILC data, run through EUROMOD rather than EUROMOD's own bundled input dataset (the EMSD), which applies EUROMOD's own harmonisation and imputation; welfare and distributional results are validated against the EUROMOD Country-Report baseline, and the effect on fiscal levels of running EU-SILC directly rather than the EMSD is unquantified (neither equivalent to a standard EUROMOD run nor inferior, only prepared differently). Every input variable a live 2023 policy reads, for which the EUROMOD input data codebook publishes a recipe for Spain and whose source fields the public EU-SILC user database carries, is populated from that recipe: 68 input columns carry a value. What is still absent is national-SILC variables, the NACE industry code which the release ships empty, and four recipes that stop short of a value. The financial capital stock IS derived, from the recipe the codebook publishes for Spain, and the IMV means test reads it; see the note on that dial, which also says why the IMV total cannot be used to check it. Spain's minimum income is calibrated to an external expenditure total, so its aggregate is a target rather than a result, and no claim about the eligibility rules underneath it rests on that aggregate. Aggregates only; no microdata.
home_html:
About the project

BENEFITS develops a Holistic Appraisal Framework (HAF) to measure the social, economic and environmental value-added of social services. HAF combines real household microdata and tax-benefit microsimulation with “beyond GDP” valuation methods to quantify how policy reforms and social services affect people's welfare. Findings are consolidated through a Social Services Policy Observatory and citizen assemblies, supported by a Visualisations Platform, and built into a Policy Evaluation Toolkit to inform policymaking.

Full title: Building Economic, Needs-Based and Environmental evaluation Frameworks for Inclusive Transformation of Social services in Europe. Coordinator: KMOP, with 10 partners across 7 countries. Funding: Horizon Europe, grant agreement no. 101179032.

About this tool

This is the Spanish edition of the Microsimulation Valuation Tool. It lets you move each reform family continuously across its modelled range and read the distributional welfare, fiscal, and provider responses for Spain. It reads a pre-computed response surface ({{POINTS_PER_DIAL}}, each already passed through the welfare layer, computed on EUROMOD ES_2023 over the EU-SILC 2024 wave) and interpolates linearly between those points as you drag a slider. It does not run the tax-benefit engine live using microdata, and ships only aggregate welfare, distributional and fiscal results, no microdata. All monetary values are in 2024 euros: 2023 nominal values uprated by the GDP deflator, ×1.0289.

The {{DIAL_COUNT}} dials

  • Minimum income (IMV, Ingreso Mínimo Vital): increases the guarantee for existing recipients by 0 to +50%. In 2023, the IMV was about €6,784 a year for a single adult.
  • Means-tested child allowance: increases the allowance by 0 to +50%. Small by construction.
  • Personal Income Tax (IRPF, Impuesto sobre la Renta de las Personas Físicas) state first-bracket rate: changes the 9.5% state rate across the modelled range, from a 5 percentage point (pp) cut to a 5pp rise. This is a rate change, not a change to the tax-free allowance; the regional (autonomic) portion is not changed.
  • Earnings downturn (market income): reduces market income by 0 to 10%, a direct earnings cut, not job losses.
  • Unemployment shock: raises unemployment by 0 to 10pp, modelled as that share of employed people losing their earnings.

One reform at a time

The tool enforces single-reform exploration: exactly one control is active at any moment, and moving any control resets the others to baseline. The response surface is calculated one reform at a time; combining two reforms is not the sum of their separate effects, because reforms interact, so the tool will not show a number it cannot stand behind.

Inequality aversion (ε)

ε sets how much more a €1 welfare gain to a lower-income household counts than the same €1 to a higher-income household. It is a value judgement you choose, not a result the tool dictates; as you change ε, the welfare figure updates to reflect it.

  • ε = 0: every €1 counts equally, regardless of income (pure efficiency; the utilitarian case).
  • ε = 1: the standard central value, a €1 gain to a household at or below the at-risk-of-poverty line counts about 1.7 times as much as the same €1 to a household on the median.
  • ε = 2: strong inequality aversion, the same gain counts about 2.8 times. That is the maximum: the living standard is floored at the at-risk-of-poverty line (AROP), 60% of the median, before the weight is taken.

A bottom-targeted reform, such as a higher minimum income guarantee, grows more valuable as ε rises; a reform whose gains sit higher up the distribution, such as a tax rate cut, shrinks as ε rises.

How to use it

Analyst mode. Set ε, then move one dial and read the results: the welfare effect, the ε strip (how that effect changes across ε values), the fiscal cost, the winners-and-losers split, and the decile chart. The other controls snap back to baseline whenever you move one.

Provider mode. Enter a caseload and targeting profile, then read the value ladder (defined below). Every value shown includes its source and provenance. The capacity-gap and shock views are indicative only. Their demand elasticities and staff ratios are registry assumptions rather than measured national figures, and the share of {{UNITS}} losing an earner is the UK's own share applied to this country's WORKING-AGE unit count, matching the base the UK measures that share on, so only that base is local.

The value ladder, a stepped set of value estimates, from the most conservative at the bottom to the fullest at the top:

  • Cash floor: the value counting only the direct cash the service moves (benefits paid or income secured). A deliberately conservative lower bound.
  • Headline: the cash floor plus the monetised value of the service's wider social outcomes, for example wellbeing gains. The main figure to quote.
  • Low/central/high band: the range around the headline, reflecting genuine uncertainty in those social-outcome values.

Scenarios mode. {{SCENARIO_COUNT_CAP}} fixed reforms and shocks, each with its fiscal cost, distributional effect, welfare, and cost-effectiveness, plus the spine, which compares the minimum income uplift with the tax cut per euro of exchequer cost rather than on their absolute effects, because the two reforms are not the same size. Per euro they are exactly equally efficient at ε = 0, where the welfare measure is just the money moved, and the uplift pulls ahead as ε rises.

Data year: EU-SILC 2024 wave; income reference year 2023; EUROMOD policy system ES_2023. Built on the EU-SILC data (2024 wave), run through EUROMOD - not EUROMOD's own bundled input dataset (the EMSD), which prepares its inputs with EUROMOD's own harmonisation and imputation. The welfare and distributional results are validated against the EUROMOD Country-Report baseline; the effect of this input difference on the fiscal figures is not quantified. Aggregates only; no microdata.

gdp_shock.label: Earnings downturn (market income)
gdp_shock.base: Market income (employees' and self-employed earnings, yem/yse in the model) is scaled down by the shown percentage; baseline is 0%. This is an across-the-board earnings cut for people in work, not job losses: everyone keeps their job but earns less.
gdp_shock.explain: An earnings downturn lowers households' incomes and the income tax and social-insurance contributions they pay, which is why it costs the exchequer (lost revenue) even though few extra benefits are triggered.
gdp_shock.winlose: Working households across the distribution lose a little earnings; the near-zero winners share is low-income households whose means-tested support rises slightly as earnings fall.

pit_give.label: IRPF state first-bracket rate change
pit_give.base: The IRPF state first-bracket rate is 9.5% (the state half of the combined 9.5% + 9.5% = 19% statutory first-bracket rate; the autonomic half is not moved). Baseline is 0 pp. The dial cuts this state rate by the shown percentage points. A tax-free-allowance dial is not offered because no single such constant is exposed in the model, so the lever is a rate cut.
pit_give.explain: Cutting the IRPF state rate returns money to income-tax payers, who sit in the middle and upper parts of the distribution, so its welfare value falls as the weight on poorer households (ε) rises.
pit_give.winlose: Winners are income-tax payers in the middle and upper-middle deciles; the poorest gain little because they pay little income tax. There are no losers.

child_benefit_up.label: Means-tested child allowance
child_benefit_up.base: Spain's means-tested child allowance, the EUROMOD bch00 instrument (a simulated benefit with three amount bands, bch00_amt4/5/6, which the shipped scenario, Child allowance +10%, scales by 10%). Baseline is 0%; the dial raises the bch00 amounts by the shown percentage. Spain has no strong universal child benefit, so this is a small, bottom-targeted instrument by construction: on the response surface a +10% uplift costs the exchequer about €100m and reaches about 2.4% of households (low-income families with children). The per-child euro amount is a policy constant of the EUROMOD ES_2023 system, which is not bundled in this deliverable, so no single figure is quoted.
child_benefit_up.explain: Raising the means-tested child allowance helps low-income families with children; the effect is small because the instrument itself is small (about 2.4% of households gain).
child_benefit_up.winlose: Winners are the roughly 2.4% of households that are low-income families with children; there are no losers. The gain is modest because the allowance is small.

min_income_up.label: Higher IMV guarantee for existing recipients
min_income_up.base: The Ingreso Mínimo Vital (IMV) minimum-income guarantee. In 2023 the IMV guarantees about €6,784 a year (€565 a month) for a single-adult household, rising with household size. Baseline is 0%. The dial raises the guaranteed payment to households already receiving IMV by the shown percentage; it holds eligibility fixed and does not model new recipients or take-up expansion.
min_income_up.explain: A higher IMV guarantee is a pure transfer to the poorest households (there are no losers), so its welfare value grows as the weight on poorer households (ε) rises.
min_income_up.winlose: Winners are the poorest households already on IMV; there are no losers, because the uplift is funded from general taxation rather than from other claimants.

unemployment_shock.label: Unemployment shock
unemployment_shock.base: Baseline is 0 pp. The dial raises unemployment by the shown percentage points, modelled as that share of employed people losing their earnings (a nested les-flip for monotonicity).
unemployment_shock.explain: A rise in unemployment removes earnings from the people who lose their jobs. NOTE: the modelled fiscal cost excludes the contributory unemployment-benefit response and therefore understates the true cost (see the caveat on the fiscal figure).
unemployment_shock.winlose: Losers are the households pushed out of work; the small winners share is households the benefit system more than compensates for a modest earnings loss. The exchequer cost shown excludes the contributory unemployment-benefit response, so the two cards read together honestly: the les-flip removes earnings but does not confer unemployment-benefit eligibility.

profiles_provenance_note: Targeting bands defined as decile groups (1 to 3, 4 to 6, and all ten). A presentational choice about which part of the distribution a service serves, with no source; the user selects among them.

scenarios.label: Baseline (current system)
scenarios.desc: The current Spanish tax-benefit system, no reform. All effects are measured against this.

scenarios.label: Unemployment +3pp
scenarios.desc: Unemployment rises by 3 percentage points; that share of employed people lose their earnings.
scenarios.winlose: Losers are the households pushed out of work; the small winners share is households the benefit system more than compensates for a modest earnings loss.

scenarios.label: Unemployment +5pp
scenarios.winlose: Losers are the newly-unemployed households; a few gain where means-tested support more than offsets the earnings lost.

scenarios.label: Earnings downturn -1%
scenarios.desc: Market earnings fall 1% across earners (an earnings cut, not job losses).
scenarios.winlose: Almost everyone in work loses a little earnings; the tiny winners share is low-income households whose means-tested support rises as earnings fall.

scenarios.label: Earnings downturn -3%
scenarios.winlose: Working households lose earnings across the distribution; near-zero winners.

scenarios.label: Earnings downturn -5%
scenarios.winlose: A broad earnings loss for working households; near-zero winners.

scenarios.label: Higher IMV guarantee +10%
scenarios.desc: The IMV minimum-income guarantee for existing recipients rises 10% (no take-up expansion).
scenarios.winlose: Winners are the low-income households already receiving IMV; near-zero losers because the uplift is funded from general taxation, not from other claimants.

scenarios.label: Higher IMV guarantee +25%
scenarios.desc: The IMV guarantee for existing recipients rises 25%.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are existing IMV recipients in the lowest deciles; near-zero losers (funded from general taxation).

scenarios.label: Higher IMV guarantee +50%
scenarios.desc: The IMV guarantee for existing recipients rises 50%. Spine scenario.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are the poorest households on IMV; there are no losers because the uplift is funded from general taxation.

scenarios.label: IRPF state first-bracket -1pp
scenarios.desc: The IRPF state first-bracket rate (9.5%) is cut by 1pp. Spine scenario.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are income-tax payers in the middle and upper-middle deciles; the poorest gain little because they pay little income tax. No losers.

scenarios.label: IRPF state first-bracket -2pp
scenarios.desc: The IRPF state first-bracket rate is cut by 2pp.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are income-tax payers up the distribution; the very bottom gains little. No losers.

scenarios.label: IRPF state first-bracket -5pp
scenarios.desc: The IRPF state first-bracket rate is cut by 5pp.
scenarios.winlose: A broad income-tax cut; gains concentrated in middle and upper deciles. No losers.

scenarios.label: Child allowance +10%
scenarios.desc: The means-tested child allowance (bch00) rises 10% (small by construction).
scenarios.winlose: Winners are low-income families with children; the effect is small because the instrument itself is small. No losers.

services.name: Employment support
services.flag: Closest available estimate: 0.46 WELLBY at the €14,050 spine (HM Treasury Wellbeing Guidance 2021: £13,000 at 2019 prices, uprated and PPP-adjusted); transferred from the UK Britain fixed-effects unemployment-to-employment coefficient as no Spanish figure exists. That gives €6,463 for one person moving into work, within a €4,972 to €7,955 band. THAT IS NOT THE VALUE THIS TOOL APPLIES: it is the wellbeing figure before the two valuation stages. The tool applies €427 per person re-employed, within a €109 to €988 band, being that figure times an effect share of 0.30 (0.11 low, 0.46 high) and an attribution of 0.22 (0.20 low, 0.27 high). Both quantities are per person re-employed, which is why the smaller one is named here: quoting €6,463 as the value overstates it about fifteenfold. The stages, their sources and every denominator are on the value's own note.

Transfer with a stated adjustment. ORIGIN 16300 FACTOR 0.39649286; BAND ORIGIN 12540 AND 20064; STAGE EFFECT 0.11 0.30 0.46 ATTRIBUTION 0.20 0.22 0.27. The origin is the UK WELLBY spine at 2024 prices and its low and high tiers; the factor is the household-final-consumption PPP to Spain, 0.861941, times the 0.46 coefficient. The stages apply in all four tools. An attribution share is the tool's convention rather than a national fact, so it needs no national warrant; the effect share is an empirical value borrowed between countries and is flagged as such below. EFFECT SHARE, an OUTCOME RATE, and a BORROWED one: 0.30 central from the Work and Health Programme job-outcome rate of 31 per cent and the Restart Scheme rate of 30 per cent, 0.11 low from Additional Work Coach Support, 0.46 high from the Work and Health Programme first-earnings rate. These are BRITISH PROGRAMME RATES APPLIED WITHOUT NATIONAL ADJUSTMENT, on a denominator of programme starts. No equivalent national rate exists for this country, and the national active labour market policy evidence is carried as a qualitative warrant only, with no effect size, by the project's own standing rule. ATTRIBUTION, an IMPACT: 0.22 central within a sourced range of 0.20, the Department for Work and Pensions' own Restart additionality projection of six in a hundred over the thirty in a hundred reaching a job outcome THE SIX IN A HUNDRED IS THE DEPARTMENT'S OWN BUSINESS-CASE PROJECTION AND NOT A STATISTICAL FINDING. It is published in House of Commons Committee of Public Accounts, The Restart Scheme for Long-term Unemployed People, Forty-Second Report of Session 2022-23, HC 733, 22 March 2023, at Conclusions and recommendations paragraph 1, where the committee quotes the Department's expectation of a return of 2.44 pounds for every pound spent and its estimate that an extra six in a hundred participants will find sustained work above what would have happened anyway, and warns in the same sentence that if that estimate is too high the benefits of the scheme will quickly fall away. The committee measured nothing here; it is reporting what the Department expected., and 0.27, the three-percentage-point Additional Work Coach Support impact over its eleven per cent in-work rate. THE PUBLICATION IS Department for Work and Pensions, The impact of additional Jobcentre Plus support on the employment outcomes of disabled people, research and analysis, 18 March 2025, which states that twelve months after the intervention 11 per cent of participants were in work compared to 8 per cent of the comparison group, a 3 percentage point employment impact, and that the impact is statistically significant. meta.poverty_basis: Two thresholds, both emitted at every point. RELATIVE (relative_*): 60% of that point's own weighted median equivalised (OECD-modified) household disposable income, the published AROP convention and the same line the social weight uses as its floor; it moves with the reform, so a reform that lowers the median lowers the line and can cut the measured count without raising anyone's income. ANCHORED (anchored_*): the same 60%-of-median line computed once at the zero-magnitude baseline point and held fixed across every point of every dial, emitted as anchored_bhc_threshold_cur so it is auditable; internally defined, needing no external source, and the right comparison of a reform against its own baseline. ANCHORED IS NOT ABSOLUTE: the absolute_* fields mean a fixed EXTERNAL base year and stay null because no sourced one exists for ES, IT or EL. The AHC fields are null throughout because the EUROMOD per-unit layer carries no housing-cost concept. All other field names follow the UK surface exactly.
meta.rebuild: Built on EUROMOD v3.8.6, on a COMPLETED input conversion. Every input variable a live 2023 policy reads, for which the EUROMOD input data codebook publishes a recipe and whose sources the public EU-SILC user database carries, is populated from that recipe: Spain carries 68 populated input columns, Greece 55, Italy 44. The consequential ones are Spain's pension and unemployment decompositions and its rent, mortgage and private-pension deductions; Greece's property tax, which is the ENFIA the model reads and passes through; and Italy's contract class, without which no employer contribution fires at all. A surface is a function of its inputs, so reproducing a stored surface is not the test; the test is agreement with each country's own published EUROMOD baseline, recorded in europe/docs/BASELINE_VALIDATION.md. Conventions this surface holds: the stable sort in build_grid.point_from_pu and in wevm._weighted_median / wevm.wevm_by_decile, the two-sided pit_give grid, and the fiscal and poverty objects emitted in the same pass, fiscal by the method of re_emit.py. min_income_up.detail: The asset test behind this dial is live. The IMV means test reads the household's financial capital, and this build derives it from the recipe the EUROMOD input data codebook publishes for Spain, capitalising reported investment income at the rate that recipe's own formula uses. What the aggregate can and cannot show. Spain's IMV is calibrated to an external expenditure total: EUROMOD's Benefit Calibration Adjustment is switched on for this system and dataset, and its target is the EUR 2,504m the Ministry of Inclusion, Social Security and Migration publishes for 2023. The modelled outlay is set by that target by construction, so where it lands is arithmetic rather than evidence, and the aggregate cannot be used to validate the eligibility rules underneath it, this asset test included. It lands just under the target rather than on it, at EUR 2,479.3m or 99.01 per cent of it, because the adjustment accumulates spending while the running total stays at or below the figure it aims at and so can never reach it exactly. What the derivation changes is who is paid, not how much is paid. The asset test enters as an eligibility condition, and the calibration then works down the same ordering until the same monetary target is exhausted, so a live test moves the composition of the recipient set while the total stays where the target puts it. The size of that compositional change has not been measured. Why it is applied at all, and neither reason is the aggregate: the recipe is published in the EUROMOD input data codebook for Spain, so it is the model's own data team's rule rather than a convention of ours; and leaving the variable at zero is not the neutral choice, because the recipe is a capital stock inferred from investment income at an assumed return, so zero is what an infinite return would imply. Of the two available assumptions, zero is the more extreme. What remains true is that the investment income the derivation capitalises is itself under-captured, at 0.57 of the external figure in the same country report, so a household whose wealth pays little or no interest is still invisible to the test. That error is one-sided and its size is not established. The adjustment's switch state and its target are read from the model by europe/model/benefit_adjustments.py.
